claim: Triple mutant zebrafish (metrn-/-, metrnla-/-, metrnlb-/-) are viable and show no obvious morphological defects at 48 hpf.
source: In contrast to published embryonic lethal Metrn mouse mutants (Kim et al., 2014), constitutive homozygote zebrafish mutants for all three genes individually (metrn-/-; metrnla-/-; metrnlb-/-), in double (metrn-/-, metrnla-/-; metrn-/-, metrnlb-/-; metrnla-/-, metrnlb-/-) and triple (metrn-/-, metrnla-/-, metrnlb-/- or triplMut), were all viable and did not show any obvious morphological defects (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of mutant zebrafish embryos at 48 hpf, with visual evidence provided in Figure 1A showing no gross phenotypic differences between wild type and triple mutant embryos.

claim: Metrn mouse mutants exhibit early embryonic lethality.
source: In contrast to published embryonic lethal Metrn mouse mutants (Kim et al., 2014), constitutive homozygote zebrafish mutants for all three genes individually (metrn-/-; metrnla-/-; metrnlb-/-), in double (metrn-/-, metrnla-/-; metrn-/-, metrnlb-/-; metrnla-/-, metrnlb-/-) and triple (metrn-/-, metrnla-/-, metrnlb-/- or triplMut), were all viable and did not show any obvious morphological defects (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2014, which reported embryonic lethality in Metrn mouse mutants.

claim: Only 38.17% of triplMut embryos exhibited wild type-like heart looping phenotype at 48 hpf, compared to 88.43% in wild type controls.
source: Indeed, while 88.43% of the wild type control embryos had D-looped shaped hearts, only 38.17% of the triplMut embryos exhibited a WT-like heart looping phenotype (Table 1 and Figure 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from heart looping analysis presented in Table 1 and Figure 1B-C, showing myl7 expression patterns.

claim: metrn-/- and metrnla-/- single mutant embryos displayed a high proportion of randomized heart phenotypes.
source: Similarly, metrn-/- and metrnla-/- single mutant embryos displayed a high proportion of randomized heart phenotypes, whereas metrnlb-/- single mutant embryos showed a small percentage of heart looping phenotypes (Table 1 and Figure 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from heart looping analysis in single mutants presented in Table 1 and Figure 1B-C.

claim: metrnlb-/- single mutant embryos showed a small percentage of heart looping phenotypes.
source: Similarly, metrn-/- and metrnla-/- single mutant embryos displayed a high proportion of randomized heart phenotypes, whereas metrnlb-/- single mutant embryos showed a small percentage of heart looping phenotypes (Table 1 and Figure 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from heart looping analysis in metrnlb-/- mutants presented in Table 1 and Figure 1B-C.

claim: Injection of metrn and/or metrnla mRNA into one-cell stage triplMut zebrafish embryos could partially rescue the observed heart looping phenotypes.
source: The injection of metrn and/or metrnla mRNA into one-cell stage triplMut zebrafish embryos could partially rescue the observed phenotypes (Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data presented in Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D showing partial restoration of normal heart looping upon mRNA injection.

claim: 10.49% of triplMut embryos exhibited symmetrical placement of the gut and pancreas with respect to the midline.
source: Indeed, 10.49% of the triplMut embryos exhibited symmetrical placement of the gut and pancreas with respect to the midline and 9.88% situs inversus or heterotaxy phenotypes compared to wild type embryos (WT: 93.84% L–R asymmetry, 4.79% L–R symmetry and 1.37% heterotaxia; Figure 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of visceral organ positioning using gata6 expression as a marker, presented in Figure 1D-E.

claim: 9.88% of triplMut embryos showed situs inversus or heterotaxy phenotypes.
source: Indeed, 10.49% of the triplMut embryos exhibited symmetrical placement of the gut and pancreas with respect to the midline and 9.88% situs inversus or heterotaxy phenotypes compared to wild type embryos (WT: 93.84% L–R asymmetry, 4.79% L–R symmetry and 1.37% heterotaxia; Figure 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of visceral organ positioning using gata6 expression as a marker, presented in Figure 1D-E.

claim: 93.84% of wild type embryos showed left-right asymmetry in visceral organ positioning.
source: Indeed, 10.49% of the triplMut embryos exhibited symmetrical placement of the gut and pancreas with respect to the midline and 9.88% situs inversus or heterotaxy phenotypes compared to wild type embryos (WT: 93.84% L–R asymmetry, 4.79% L–R symmetry and 1.37% heterotaxia; Figure 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of visceral organ positioning in wild type embryos using gata6 expression as a marker, presented in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Metrns are not implicated in the specification of the heart or visceral organs.
source: These results indicate that while Metrns are not implicated in the specification of neither the heart nor the visceral organs (myl7 and gata6 expression being detected in triplMut embryos and in single mutants for metrns), their loss of function reveals that they are implicated in the L-R asymmetry positioning of these organs.
evidence: The claim is supported by the observation that myl7 and gata6 expression markers are detected in triplMut embryos, indicating organ specification occurs despite the absence of Metrns.

claim: Metrns are implicated in the left-right asymmetry positioning of the heart and visceral organs.
source: These results indicate that while Metrns are not implicated in the specification of neither the heart nor the visceral organs (myl7 and gata6 expression being detected in triplMut embryos and in single mutants for metrns), their loss of function reveals that they are implicated in the L-R asymmetry positioning of these organs.
evidence: The claim is supported by the observed defects in heart looping and visceral organ positioning in metrn mutants, despite normal organ specification.

claim: Nodal is a ligand belonging to the TGFβ protein family.
source: One major regulator for the establishment of the L-R axis is Nodal, a ligand belonging to the TGFβ protein family (Blum et al., 2014; Blum and Ott, 2018; Grimes and Burdine, 2017; Kawasumi et al., 2011; Branford and Yost, 2004; Zhou et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature describing Nodal as a TGFβ family member.

claim: Nodal signaling is activated in the left lateral plate mesoderm (LPM) and remains inactive in the right LPM.
source: Its signaling is activated in the left lateral plate mesoderm (LPM), whereas Nodal remains inactive in the right LPM, creating an embryo-scale left-right asymmetry (Grimes and Burdine, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Grimes and Burdine, 2017, describing the asymmetric activation of Nodal signaling.

claim: In mice, the Node generates a leftward flow of extraembryonic fluid called the Nodal flow through oriented rotation of cilia.
source: In mice, this asymmetry is achieved by an oriented rotation of the cilia of a structure called the Node, generating a leftward flow of extraembryonic fluid named the Nodal flow.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the mechanism of left-right symmetry breaking in mice.

claim: The Nodal flow results in asymmetric expression of several Nodal factors and Nodal signaling.
source: In mice, this asymmetry is achieved by an oriented rotation of the cilia of a structure called the Node, generating a leftward flow of extraembryonic fluid named the Nodal flow. This results in an asymmetric expression of several Nodal factors and Nodal signaling.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the consequences of Nodal flow in mice.

claim: Leftys are soluble inhibitors belonging to a subclass of TGF factors that antagonize Nodal signaling.
source: Participating in this patterning, Leftys, soluble inhibitors belonging to a subclass of TGF factors, antagonize Nodal signaling (Chen and Schier, 2002; Chen and Shen, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen and Schier, 2002 and Chen and Shen, 2004, describing Lefty proteins as Nodal antagonists.

claim: In zebrafish, the Kupffer's vesicle (KV) is a key structure for left-right symmetry breaking during embryonic development.
source: For instance, in Xenopus the gastrocoel roof plate and in zebrafish the Kupffer's vesicle (KV; Essner et al., 2005; Vick et al., 2009; Nonaka et al., 2002; Schweickert et al., 2007; Okada et al., 2005; Tanaka et al., 2005) are key structures of the L-R symmetry breaking during the embryonic development (Nonaka et al., 2002; Okada et al., 2005; Nonaka et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations describing the role of the Kupffer's vesicle in zebrafish left-right patterning.

claim: In Xenopus, the gastrocoel roof plate is a key structure for left-right symmetry breaking during embryonic development.
source: For instance, in Xenopus the gastrocoel roof plate and in zebrafish the Kupffer's vesicle (KV; Essner et al., 2005; Vick et al., 2009; Nonaka et al., 2002; Schweickert et al., 2007; Okada et al., 2005; Tanaka et al., 2005) are key structures of the L-R symmetry breaking during the embryonic development (Nonaka et al., 2002; Okada et al., 2005; Nonaka et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations describing the role of the gastrocoel roof plate in Xenopus left-right patterning.

claim: In humans and other mammals like rabbits and mice, left-right body symmetry establishment begins with asymmetric fluid flow driven by rotating cilia.
source: Similarly, in humans and other mammals like rabbits and mice, the systematic establishment of left-right body symmetry begins with asymmetric fluid flow driven by rotating cilia (Smith et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2019, describing cilia-driven fluid flow in mammalian left-right patterning.

claim: The zebrafish Kupffer's vesicle is a fluid-filled sphere with a ciliated epithelium.
source: Compared to the relatively flat-shaped mouse node, the zebrafish KV is a fluid-filled sphere with a ciliated epithelium, and it is formed by dorsal forerunner cells (DFCs; Essner et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Essner et al., 2005, describing the structure of the Kupffer's vesicle.

claim: The Kupffer's vesicle is formed by dorsal forerunner cells (DFCs).
source: Compared to the relatively flat-shaped mouse node, the zebrafish KV is a fluid-filled sphere with a ciliated epithelium, and it is formed by dorsal forerunner cells (DFCs; Essner et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Essner et al., 2005, describing the cellular origin of the Kupffer's vesicle.

claim: DFCs first emerge as cells of the epithelium of the dorsal surface in direct contact with the yolk syncytial layer at 6 hours post-fertilization (hpf).
source: DFCs first emerge as cells of the epithelium of the dorsal surface in direct contact with the yolk syncytial layer at 6 hours post-fertilization (hpf; Oteíza et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Oteíza et al., 2008, describing the emergence of DFCs.

claim: Around 8-9 hpf, 20-30 DFCs form a single cluster and migrate towards the vegetal pole.
source: Around 8–9 hpf, following the epibolic movement, 20–30 DFCs form a single cluster and migrate towards the vegetal pole in a non-involuting manner at the leading edge (Oteíza et al., 2008; Cooper and D'Amico, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Oteíza et al., 2008 and Cooper and D'Amico, 1996, describing DFC clustering and migration.

claim: The KV is formed by 12 hpf.
source: The focal points of the cluster are then rearranged by integrating the unpolarized DFCs to form a single focal point that will expand into a monolayer rosette structure containing a lumen to form the KV by 12 hpf (Essner et al., 2005; Oteíza et al., 2008; Cooper and D'Amico, 1996; Pulgar et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations describing the timeline of KV formation.

claim: Non-motile and motile monocilia are generated on the apical membrane of KV cells facing the lumen.
source: Along this process, non-motile and motile monocilia are generated on the apical membrane facing the lumen that create a counterclockwise flow of fluid by the KV, called Nodal flow (Oteíza et al., 2008; Kramer-Zucker et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Oteíza et al., 2008 and Kramer-Zucker et al., 2005, describing cilia formation in the KV.

claim: The leftward-directed flow within the KV results in asymmetric expression of zebrafish Nodal genes, like spaw, lefty1, and lefty2.
source: It was shown that the leftward-directed flow within the KV results in asymmetric expression of zebrafish Nodal genes, like spaw, lefty1, and lefty2, which is fundamental for proper L-R patterning (Hirokawa et al., 2006; Harvey, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hirokawa et al., 2006 and Harvey, 1998, describing the relationship between KV flow and Nodal gene expression.

claim: Meteorin (Metrn) was hypothesized to be a novel important regulator of Nodal transcription.
source: In this context, it has been reported that nodal, lefty, as well as p-smad2 expression is downregulated in Meteorin-null ES cells. As such, Meteorin (Metrn) was hypothesized to be a novel important regulator of Nodal transcription (Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2014, which reported downregulation of nodal pathway components in Meteorin-null ES cells.

claim: Meteorin (Metrn) is a secreted neurotrophic factor highly conserved among vertebrates.
source: Meteorin (Metrn), a secreted neurotrophic factor highly conserved among vertebrates, is expressed during early mouse development.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Meteorin protein characteristics.

claim: Meteorin is expressed during early mouse development, detected at the blastocyst stage in the inner cell mass.
source: Meteorin (Metrn), a secreted neurotrophic factor highly conserved among vertebrates, is expressed during early mouse development. It is already detected at the blastocyst stage in the inner cell mass and then expands through the extraembryonic ectoderm to the central (CNS) and peripheral nervous system (PNS) during later developmental stages (Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2014, describing Meteorin expression during mouse development.

claim: Meteorin was first described to induce glial cell differentiation and promote axonal extension in dorsal root ganglion (DRG) explants in vitro.
source: It was first described to induce glial cell differentiation and to promote axonal extension in dorsal root ganglion (DRG) explants in vitro (Nishino et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nishino et al., 2004, describing the initial functional characterization of Meteorin.

claim: The disruption of Metrn function in mice resulted in early embryonic lethality.
source: The disruption of Metrn function in mice resulted in early embryonic lethality (Kim et al., 2014), preventing the investigation of Metrn protein function during early embryonic development in vivo and, in particular, their role in L-R patterning.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2014, reporting embryonic lethality in Metrn mouse mutants.

claim: Meteorin-like (Metrnl) was first reported as a downstream target of the Pax2/5/8 signaling pathway during otic vesicle development.
source: Also conserved among vertebrates, its paralog Meteorin-like (Metrnl) has been first reported as a downstream target of the Pax2/5/8 signaling pathway during otic vesicle development (Ramialison et al., 2008) and was later shown to have neurotrophic properties comparable to the ones of Metrn (Jørgensen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ramialison et al., 2008, describing Metrnl as a Pax2/5/8 target.

claim: Meteorin-like (Metrnl) has neurotrophic properties comparable to Metrn.
source: Also conserved among vertebrates, its paralog Meteorin-like (Metrnl) has been first reported as a downstream target of the Pax2/5/8 signaling pathway during otic vesicle development (Ramialison et al., 2008) and was later shown to have neurotrophic properties comparable to the ones of Metrn (Jørgensen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jørgensen et al., 2012, describing the neurotrophic properties of Metrnl.

claim: No metrn or metrnla expression could be detected in triplMut embryos by in situ hybridization from two-cell stage to 1 day post-fertilization.
source: To do so, we performed in situ hybridization on metrn, metrnla, and metrnlb from two-cell stage to 1 day post-fertilization (dpf) on triplMut embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B). No expression could be detected for neither of those two genes in the triplMut embryos, indicating the degradation of the transcripts in the metrn mutant backgrounds (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B demonstrating absence of metrn and metrnla transcripts in triplMut embryos.

claim: A significant reduction in the expression of all metrn genes was measured in triplMut samples by qRT-PCR.
source: To confirm this observation, we compared the expression level of all three metrn genes upon total mRNA extraction from 14 and 48 hpf WT and triplMut embryos by qRT-PCR. Metrn and metrnla expression was detected in samples of 14 hpf WT embryos, and metrnlb expression was detected in samples of 48 hpf WT embryos. A significant reduction in the expression of all metrn genes could be measured using triplMut samples of the same age.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data comparing metrn gene expression levels between WT and triplMut embryos.

claim: The mRNA produced by the targeted metrn loci is degraded by nonsense-mediated decay.
source: A significant reduction in the expression of all metrn genes could be measured using triplMut samples of the same age. These results suggest that the mRNA produced by the loci that we targeted is degraded by nonsense-mediated decay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the significant reduction in metrn gene expression in mutants, consistent with nonsense-mediated decay of transcripts containing premature stop codons.

claim: dand5 expression at 14 hpf is significantly reduced in triplMut embryos compared to wild type controls.
source: By qRT-PCR, we measured a significant reduction of dand5 expression at 14 hpf in triplMut embryos compared to wild type controls (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A demonstrating reduced dand5 expression in triplMut embryos.

claim: The expression of spaw, lft1, and lft2 is downregulated in triplMut embryos compared to wild type embryos.
source: Similarly, the expression of spaw, lft1, as well as lft2, in the absence of Metrns proteins was also downregulated in triplMut embryos compared to wild type embryos (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A demonstrating reduced expression of Nodal pathway genes in triplMut embryos.

claim: In metrn-/- and metrnla-/- single mutants and triplMut embryos, spaw expression could not be detected in the left LPM and was only faintly detected around the KV at 16 hpf.
source: At 16 hpf, spaw is normally expressed adjacent to the KV and in the left LPM. In metrn-/- and metrnla-/- single mutants as well as triplMut embryos, we could not detect any spaw expression in the left LPM and only faintly around the KV (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B demonstrating altered spaw expression patterns in metrn mutants.

claim: lft1 expression at the midline was severely disrupted in all analyzed metrn mutants at 16 hpf.
source: The spaw inhibitor lft1 at this stage is expressed along the midline. In all analyzed metrn mutants (single metrn and metrnla and triplMut), its expression was severely disrupted at the midline (Figure 2B, middle panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B demonstrating disrupted lft1 expression in metrn mutants.

claim: lft2 expression in the left heart field was either absent or randomized in metrn mutants at 16 hpf.
source: The same was observed for lft2, which expression in the left heart field was either absent or randomized in metrn mutants, single or triplMut embryos, compared to the wild type embryos (Figure 2B, lower panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B demonstrating altered lft2 expression in metrn mutants.

claim: In more than 61% of triplMut embryos, particularly reduced dand5 expression was detected at 14 hpf.
source: In more than 61% triplMut embryos, we could detect particularly reduced dand5 expression at 14 hpf, and 23% displayed an abnormal dand5 R>L expression bias (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data and quantification shown in Figure 2C-D demonstrating reduced dand5 expression in triplMut embryos.

claim: 23% of triplMut embryos displayed an abnormal dand5 R>L expression bias at 14 hpf.
source: In more than 61% triplMut embryos, we could detect particularly reduced dand5 expression at 14 hpf, and 23% displayed an abnormal dand5 R>L expression bias (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data and quantification shown in Figure 2C-D demonstrating abnormal dand5 expression patterns in triplMut embryos.

claim: dand5 expression pattern was altered in single metrn-/- and metrnla-/- mutant embryos.
source: In single metrn-/- and metrnla-/- mutant embryos, dand5 expression pattern was also altered (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 demonstrating altered dand5 expression in single mutants.

claim: dand5 expression in the KV is only altered if upstream symmetry-breaking mechanisms are disrupted.
source: These results are in line with previous findings reporting that dand5 expression in the KV is only altered if upstream symmetry-breaking mechanisms are disrupted (Pelliccia et al., 2017; Hojo et al., 2007; Gourronc et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pelliccia et al., 2017, Hojo et al., 2007, and Gourronc et al., 2007, describing the relationship between dand5 expression and upstream symmetry-breaking mechanisms.

claim: Both metrn and metrnla are maternally expressed at the two-cell stage.
source: At the two-cell stage, we detected both metrn and metrnla maternally expressed transcripts, whereas metrnlb expression was not detected (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A demonstrating maternal expression of metrn and metrnla.

claim: metrnlb expression was not detected at the two-cell stage.
source: At the two-cell stage, we detected both metrn and metrnla maternally expressed transcripts, whereas metrnlb expression was not detected (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A showing absence of metrnlb expression at early stages.

claim: The earliest time point for zygotic expression of metrn and metrnla was at 6 hpf (shield stage).
source: The earliest time point for zygotic expression of metrn and metrnla was at 6 hpf (shield stage).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization analysis tracking the onset of zygotic metrn and metrnla expression.

claim: At 6 hpf, metrnla expression could be detected over the whole animal cap.
source: At this stage, metrnla expression could be detected over the whole animal cap, whereas zygotic metrn expression onset was observed only around the yolk syncytial layer (YSL) at this developmental stage (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A demonstrating metrnla expression pattern at 6 hpf.

claim: At 6 hpf, zygotic metrn expression was observed only around the yolk syncytial layer (YSL).
source: At this stage, metrnla expression could be detected over the whole animal cap, whereas zygotic metrn expression onset was observed only around the yolk syncytial layer (YSL) at this developmental stage (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A demonstrating metrn expression pattern at 6 hpf.

claim: From 9 hpf, metrn expression was restricted to the developing LPM and to the leading edge of the former shield area.
source: Metrn expression was then restricted to the developing LPM and to the leading edge of the former shield area from 9 hpf (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B demonstrating metrn expression pattern at 9 hpf.

claim: metrnla was expressed throughout the whole enveloping layer and developing midline from 9 hpf.
source: In comparison, metrnla was found expressed throughout the whole enveloping layer and developing midline (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B demonstrating metrnla expression pattern at 9 hpf.

claim: At 12 hpf, metrn expression was restricted to the KV area.
source: At 12 hpf, the expression of metrn was restricted to the KV area while metrnla transcripts were mainly found in the midline (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization and HCR data shown in Figure 3A-B demonstrating metrn expression at 12 hpf.

claim: At 12 hpf, metrnla transcripts were mainly found in the midline.
source: At 12 hpf, the expression of metrn was restricted to the KV area while metrnla transcripts were mainly found in the midline (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization and HCR data shown in Figure 3A-B demonstrating metrnla expression at 12 hpf.

claim: At 14 hpf, metrn expression was present in the KV area and in the developing brain.
source: By 14 hpf, metrn expression was present in the KV area as well as in the developing brain, whereas metrnla transcripts were mainly found in the midline and the KV area (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B demonstrating metrn expression at 14 hpf.

claim: At 14 hpf, metrnla transcripts were mainly found in the midline and the KV area.
source: By 14 hpf, metrn expression was present in the KV area as well as in the developing brain, whereas metrnla transcripts were mainly found in the midline and the KV area (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B demonstrating metrnla expression at 14 hpf.

claim: No metrnlb transcripts could be detected from the two-cell stage to 14 hpf.
source: In contrast, from the two-cell stage to 14 hpf, no metrnlb transcripts could be detected (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B showing absence of metrnlb expression at early stages.

claim: metrn and metrnla expression colocalize in the area of the KV at 12 and 14 hpf.
source: By HCR, we found metrn and metrnla expression colocalizing in the area of the KV at 12 and 14 hpf (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by HCR data shown in Figure 3B demonstrating colocalization of metrn and metrnla expression in the KV region.

claim: By 24 and 48 hpf, both metrn and metrnla were strongly expressed in the CNS.
source: By 24 and 48 hpf, both genes were found strongly expressed in the CNS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C demonstrating CNS expression of metrn and metrnla at later stages.

claim: metrnlb expression onset started from 24 hpf broadly in the embryonic brain.
source: Finally, metrnlb expression onset started from 24 hpf broadly in the embryonic brain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C demonstrating metrnlb expression at 24 hpf.

claim: At 48 hpf, metrnlb transcripts were mostly found in the otic vesicles and at the somite boundaries.
source: At 48 hpf, metrnlb transcripts were mostly found in the otic vesicles and at the somite boundaries (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C demonstrating metrnlb expression pattern at 48 hpf.

claim: metrn and sox32 are co-expressed by dorsal forerunner cells (DFCs) at 10 hpf.
source: We observed a complete colocalization of metrn/sox32 and metrnla/sox32 signals at 10 hpf, indicating that metrns genes are expressed in DFCs, the cells that will later form the KV (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by double fluorescence in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3C demonstrating colocalization of metrn and sox32 in DFCs.

claim: metrnla and sox32 are co-expressed by dorsal forerunner cells (DFCs) at 10 hpf.
source: We observed a complete colocalization of metrn/sox32 and metrnla/sox32 signals at 10 hpf, indicating that metrns genes are expressed in DFCs, the cells that will later form the KV (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by double fluorescence in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3D demonstrating colocalization of metrnla and sox32 in DFCs.

claim: metrn and metrnla are expressed at the Hensen's node and around the primitive streak in chick embryos at stage HH6.
source: Around stage HH6, we could observe metrn and metrnla expression at the Hensen's node and around the primitive streak (marked by primitive streak landmark fgf8; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data in chick embryos shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D demonstrating metrn and metrnla expression at the node.

claim: metrn gene expression at early developmental stages in embryonic Node and midline structures is conserved throughout vertebrates.
source: Remarkably, the chick metrn and metrnla expression patterns were reminiscent of the ones that we observed in zebrafish, suggesting that metrn gene expression at early developmental stages in embryonic Node and midline structures is conserved throughout vertebrates.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the similar expression patterns of metrn genes in zebrafish and chick embryos at node/KV structures.

claim: About 65% of triplMut embryos displayed multiple segregated DFC clusters or abnormal linear cellular distributions at 9 and 10 hpf.
source: Compared to wild type embryos displaying ovoid DFC clustering, about 65% of the triplMut embryos displayed multiple segregated DFC clusters or abnormal linear cellular distributions as shown using sox32 marker in 9 and 10 hpf triplMut embryos (Figure 4A-B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data and quantification shown in Figure 4A-B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, and Table 2 demonstrating DFC clustering defects in triplMut embryos.

claim: metrn-/- and metrnla-/- single mutant embryos presented clustering defects of sox32-expressing DFCs.
source: Similarly, metrn-/- as well as metrnla-/- single mutant embryos presented clustering defects of sox32-expressing DFC compared to wild type embryos (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B, Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data and quantification shown in Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B, and Table 2 demonstrating DFC clustering defects in single mutants.

claim: In single or triplMut+/- heterozygous embryos, DFC clustering was not significantly or very mildly affected.
source: In single or triplMut+/- heterozygous embryos, the DFC clustering was instead not significantly or very mildly affected as revealed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Table 2 demonstrating minimal DFC clustering defects in heterozygous embryos.

claim: tbxta and sox17 DFC markers are expressed in the absence of Metrn proteins.
source: The observed defects were also present when using tbxta and sox17 as DFC markers whose expression was detected at 8 and 10 hpf respectively, indicating that although disorganized, the DFC identity was not altered by the absence of metrns expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C demonstrating expression of DFC markers in triplMut embryos.

claim: DFC identity is not altered by the absence of metrns expression.
source: The observed defects were also present when using tbxta and sox17 as DFC markers whose expression was detected at 8 and 10 hpf respectively, indicating that although disorganized, the DFC identity was not altered by the absence of metrns expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the continued expression of DFC-specific markers (tbxta and sox17) in triplMut embryos despite clustering defects.

claim: DFCs in triplMut embryos showed migratory delays of about 8% to 13% at 6 hpf, 8 hpf, and 10 hpf compared to wild type embryos.
source: Compared to wild type embryos, DFCs in triplMut embryos showed migratory delays of about 8% to 13% at all analyzed developmental stages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C, Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of DFC migration distance shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C and Table 3.

claim: triplMut DFCs exhibited a diminished convergence rate compared to wild type control DFCs.
source: In line with the DFC clustering abnormalities in fixed triplMut embryos that we observed, the tracking of these cells in triplMut embryos versus wild type control embryos revealed a diminished convergence rate for triplMut DFCs (Figure 4E, upper panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging and tracking data shown in Figure 4E demonstrating reduced convergence of DFCs in triplMut embryos.

claim: triplMut DFCs showed a significant decrease in migration speed compared to wild type DFCs.
source: Furthermore, we measured a significant decrease in their migration speed compared to the wild type DFCs (Figure 4E, lower panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging and tracking data shown in Figure 4E demonstrating reduced migration speed of DFCs in triplMut embryos.

claim: Individually tracked DFCs exhibited consistent movement toward the vegetal pole regardless of the absence of Metrns proteins.
source: Intriguingly, individually tracked DFCs exhibited a consistent movement toward the vegetal pole, regardless of the absence of Metrns proteins (Figure 4D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, Figure 4—videos 1; 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging and tracking data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D demonstrating directional migration of DFCs in triplMut embryos.

claim: The absence of Metrn proteins does not affect DFC migration directionality but alters their migratory abilities, including migration speed and convergence rate.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that the absence of Metrn proteins does not affect DFC migration directionality but alters instead their migratory abilities, including migration speed and convergence rate.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations that DFCs in triplMut embryos maintain directional migration but show reduced speed and convergence.

claim: During epiboly, initial EVL cells destined to develop into DFCs exhibit an accumulation of ZO-1 along their apical junctions.
source: It was shown that during the process of epiboly, initial EVL cells destined to develop into DFCs exhibit an accumulation of ZO-1 along their apical junctions. Subsequently, their apical surface gradually diminishes in size, resulting in the formation of discrete apical domains enriched with ZO-1 (Oteíza et al., 2008; Pulgar et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Oteíza et al., 2008 and Pulgar et al., 2021, describing ZO-1 accumulation during DFC development.

claim: At 6 and 8 hpf, triplMut GFP-positive DFCs exhibited reduced ZO-1 enrichment at their apical junctions compared to wild type controls.
source: As expected, immunohistochemistry against ZO-1 on 6 and 8 hpf Tg(sox17:GFP) wild type control embryos where DFCs are labeled with GFP was enriched in ZO-1 at their apical side and apical junctions (Figure 4F-G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E). At this same developmental stage, a reduced ZO-1 enrichment at the apical junctions of triplMut GFP-positive DFCs could be detected (Figure 4F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E left plot). Similarly, at 8 hpf, GFP-positive triplMut DFCs exhibited diminished ZO-1 at their apical region (Figure 4G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E right plot).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4F-G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E demonstrating reduced ZO-1 enrichment in triplMut DFCs.

claim: triplMut GFP-positive DFCs appear to have lost their apical attachments to the EVL.
source: Furthermore, compared to wild type DFCs, triplMut GFP-positive DFCs appear to have lost their apical attachments to the EVL (Figure 4F–G, right panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4F-G demonstrating detachment of triplMut DFCs from the EVL.

claim: The distance between triplMut DFCs and the EVL/YSL at 6 and 8 hpf was significantly higher compared to wild type DFCs.
source: Indeed, the distance measured between triplMut DFCs and the EVL/YSL at 6 and 8 hpf was significantly higher compared to the one of wild type DFCs (6 hpf: *p-value: 0.039, N=4 WT, 30 DFCs measured, triplMut N=6, 46 DFCs measured; 8 hpf: *p-value: 0.021, N=7 WT embryos, 47 DFCs measured, N=7 triplMut, 54 DFCs measured; Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of DFC-EVL distance shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The Kupffer's vesicle is a ciliated organ transiently present from around 10.5 hpf to 30 hpf.
source: At the end of gastrulation, DFCs that migrated to deeper layers of the developing zebrafish embryo form a lumen to shape the KV, a ciliated organ transiently present (from around 10.5 hpf to 30 hpf Kimmel et al., 1995) that is crucial for initiating L-R asymmetric patterning (Essner et al., 2005; Cooper and D'Amico, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kimmel et al., 1995, describing the temporal presence of the Kupffer's vesicle.

claim: Dand5 is expressed adjacent to the KV with a right-left (R>L) bias between 11 and 14 hpf in zebrafish.
source: As we observed at 14 hpf, it was reported that Dand5, a member of the Cerberus/Dan family of secreted factors, is expressed adjacent to the KV with a right – left (R>L) bias between 11 and 14 hpf in zebrafish (Figure 2; Hashimoto et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hashimoto et al., 2004, describing dand5 expression pattern near the KV.

claim: The right-biased expression of dand5 is directly influenced by the direction and strength of the Nodal flow generated by the KV.
source: The right-biased expression of dand5 was shown to be directly influenced by the direction and the strength of the Nodal flow generated by the KV (Sampaio et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sampaio et al., 2014, describing the relationship between Nodal flow and dand5 expression.

claim: Dand5 contributes to the left-biased expression of spaw in the LPM by antagonizing Spaw activity.
source: In return, Dand5 contributes to the left-biased expression of spaw in the LPM by antagonizing Spaw activity (Hashimoto et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hashimoto et al., 2004, describing the role of Dand5 in regulating spaw expression.

claim: triplMut embryos displayed a significant reduction in KV cell number at 14 hpf compared to wild type controls.
source: We then measured the number of cells in the KV, the KV diameter, and the number of cilia, which were correlating with the number of cells, of both wild type and triplMut embryos (Figure 5B-D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). Previous work has shown that the KV diameter and the number of KV cilia cells, as well as KV cilia, can be highly variable from embryo to embryo (Gokey et al., 2016). Nevertheless, despite the wide variability, we observed highly significant reduction in all cases (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of KV cell number shown in Figure 5B demonstrating reduced cell numbers in triplMut embryos.

claim: triplMut embryos displayed a significant reduction in KV diameter at 14 hpf compared to wild type controls.
source: We then measured the number of cells in the KV, the KV diameter, and the number of cilia, which were correlating with the number of cells, of both wild type and triplMut embryos (Figure 5B-D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). Previous work has shown that the KV diameter and the number of KV cilia cells, as well as KV cilia, can be highly variable from embryo to embryo (Gokey et al., 2016). Nevertheless, despite the wide variability, we observed highly significant reduction in all cases (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of KV diameter shown in Figure 5C demonstrating reduced KV size in triplMut embryos.

claim: triplMut embryos displayed a significant reduction in the number of KV cilia at 14 hpf compared to wild type controls.
source: We then measured the number of cells in the KV, the KV diameter, and the number of cilia, which were correlating with the number of cells, of both wild type and triplMut embryos (Figure 5B-D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). Previous work has shown that the KV diameter and the number of KV cilia cells, as well as KV cilia, can be highly variable from embryo to embryo (Gokey et al., 2016). Nevertheless, despite the wide variability, we observed highly significant reduction in all cases (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cilia number shown in Figure 5D demonstrating reduced cilia numbers in triplMut embryos.

claim: triplMut embryos displayed a significant reduction in KV cilia length at 14 hpf compared to wild type controls.
source: In addition, compared to the wild type controls, triplMut embryos also displayed a significant reduction in the KV cilia length (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cilia length shown in Figure 5E demonstrating reduced cilia length in triplMut embryos.

claim: By 14 hpf, DFCs clustering into a rosette structure lead tight junctions to form the KV lumen.
source: As described recently and observed in ZO-1 stained embryos, by 14 hpf, DFCs clustering into a rosette structure lead tight junctions to form the KV lumen (Oteíza et al., 2008; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Oteíza et al., 2008 and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A describing KV lumen formation.

claim: ZO-1 immunostained triplMut embryos at 14 hpf displayed an irregular ZO-1 lattice pattern and disrupted KV lumen shape.
source: In contrast, ZO-1 immunostained triplMut embryos of the same developmental stage displayed an irregular ZO-1 lattice pattern and disrupted KV lumen shape (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A demonstrating disrupted KV lumen in triplMut embryos.

claim: triplMut embryos displayed only partially polarized DFCs indicated by absent or irregular aPKC-ζ immunolabeling at 14 hpf.
source: Additionally, unlike in control embryos, triplMut embryos displayed only partially polarized DFCs indicated by absent or irregular aPKC-ζ immunolabeling (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B demonstrating reduced DFC polarization in triplMut embryos.

claim: The loss of Metrns function impacts proper DFC polarization and subsequent KV formation.
source: These results indicate that the loss of Metrns function also impacts proper DFC polarization and subsequent KV formation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed defects in ZO-1 lattice pattern, KV lumen shape, and aPKC-ζ labeling in triplMut embryos.

claim: Beads movement analysis within the KV showed a counter-clockwise rotation of the flow in wild type control embryos.
source: Beads movement analysis within the KV showed a counter-clockwise rotation of the flow in wild type control (Figure 5F, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescent microsphere tracking data shown in Figure 5F demonstrating directional flow in wild type KV.

claim: The counter-clockwise flow movement in the KV was severely impaired in triplMut embryos.
source: In contrast, this movement was severely impaired in triplMut embryos (Figure 5F, Figure 5—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescent microsphere tracking data shown in Figure 5F demonstrating impaired flow in triplMut KV.

claim: Mean square displacement (MSD) analysis revealed a directed motion of microbeads in the wild type KV.
source: This analysis revealed a directed motion of microbeads in the wild type KV (MSD quadratic dependence on ∆t) and a confined motion (MSD asymptotic behavior) in triplMut (de Bruin et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by MSD analysis of bead trajectories showing quadratic dependence characteristic of directed motion in wild type embryos.

claim: Mean square displacement (MSD) analysis revealed a confined motion of microbeads in triplMut KV.
source: This analysis revealed a directed motion of microbeads in the wild type KV (MSD quadratic dependence on ∆t) and a confined motion (MSD asymptotic behavior) in triplMut (de Bruin et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by MSD analysis of bead trajectories showing asymptotic behavior characteristic of confined motion in triplMut embryos.

claim: Average bead velocity showed an overall reduction in the beads' speed in triplMut mutant embryos compared to wild types.
source: Accordingly, measurement of average bead velocity showed an overall reduction in the beads' speed in the triplMut mutant embryos compared to the wild types (WT mean = 0.96212 μm/s; TriplMut mean = 0.47996 μm/s; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of bead velocity shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C demonstrating reduced flow speed in triplMut embryos.

claim: The observed defects in KV formation in the absence of Metrns severely impact its function and the Nodal flow generation.
source: These results demonstrate that the observed defects in the KV formation in the absence of Metrns also severely impact its function and thereby the Nodal flow generation, responsible for proper Nodal factors expression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations of structural KV defects and impaired Nodal flow in triplMut embryos.

claim: Integrins are membrane receptors involved in cell adhesion and recognition during embryogenesis.
source: Integrins are membrane receptors involved in cell adhesion and recognition during embryogenesis, amongst others (Hynes, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hynes, 1992, describing the role of integrins in development.

claim: During gastrulation, itgαV and itgβ1b are expressed in DFCs.
source: During gastrulation, itgαV as well as itgβ1b were shown to be expressed in DFCs, and itgαV and itgβ1b morpholino-injected embryos display DFC phenotypic defects reminiscent of those observed in metrn mutants (Ablooglu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ablooglu et al., 2010, describing integrin expression in DFCs.

claim: itgαV and itgβ1b morpholino-injected embryos display DFC phenotypic defects reminiscent of those observed in metrn mutants.
source: During gastrulation, itgαV as well as itgβ1b were shown to be expressed in DFCs, and itgαV and itgβ1b morpholino-injected embryos display DFC phenotypic defects reminiscent of those observed in metrn mutants (Ablooglu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ablooglu et al., 2010, describing DFC defects in integrin morphants.

claim: No significant change in itgαV and itgβ1b expression levels was measured in triplMut embryos compared to wild type controls at 6, 9, and 24 hpf.
source: We therefore asked whether Metrns loss of function could affect the expression of both integrins. To do so, we quantified itgαV and itgβ1b expression levels in wild type and triplMut embryos at 6, 9, and 24 hpf by qRT-PCR. No significant change in itgαV and itgβ1b expression levels at either tested developmental stage was measured in triplMut embryos compared to wild type controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A demonstrating no change in integrin expression in triplMut embryos.

claim: A significantly higher percentage of embryos with DFC clustering defects was observed upon injection of low doses of itgβ1b or itgαV1 morpholino into triplMut+/- embryos.
source: Instead, the injection of low doses of either itgβ1b or itgαV1 morpholino did not affect DFC clustering, similarly to non-injected triplMut+/- embryos (Figure 6A, Table 4). However, a significantly higher percentage of embryos with DFC clustering defects could be observed upon the injection of either morpholino at low dose into triplMut+/- (Figure 6A, Table 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of DFC clustering defects shown in Figure 6A and Table 4 demonstrating genetic interaction between metrns and integrins.

claim: Metrn proteins act together with Integrins ItgαV1 and Itgβ1b for the proper clustering and migration of DFCs during early embryonic development without directly affecting their expression.
source: These results are consistent with the hypothesis that Metrn proteins act together with both Integrins for the proper clustering and migration of DFCs during early embryonic development without directly affecting their expression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic interaction data showing enhanced DFC defects when combining metrn heterozygosity with low-dose integrin morpholinos, without changes in integrin expression.

claim: Proteins of the Meteorin family were first described as secreted neurotrophic factors highly conserved among vertebrates.
source: Proteins of the Meteorin family were first described as secreted neurotrophic factors highly conserved among vertebrates (Kim et al., 2014; Nishino et al., 2004; Ramialison et al., 2008; Jørgensen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations describing Meteorin proteins as conserved neurotrophic factors.

claim: Metrnla mutant mice display phenotypes including impaired angiogenesis after ischemic injury.
source: In mice, Metrnla mutants display phenotypes as impaired angiogenesis after ischemic injury (Reboll et al., 2022) or dysregulated cytokine production (Ushach et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reboll et al., 2022, describing angiogenesis defects in Metrnla mutants.

claim: Metrnla mutant mice display dysregulated cytokine production.
source: In mice, Metrnla mutants display phenotypes as impaired angiogenesis after ischemic injury (Reboll et al., 2022) or dysregulated cytokine production (Ushach et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ushach et al., 2018, describing cytokine dysregulation in Metrnla mutants.

claim: Metrns are required for symmetry breaking and the establishment of left-right asymmetry.
source: Our results demonstrate that Metrns are required for symmetry breaking and the establishment of L-R asymmetry, a novel role for Meteorin proteins during vertebrate embryonic development.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined experimental data showing heart looping defects, visceral organ positioning defects, and altered Nodal gene expression in metrn mutants.

claim: All three metrn paralogs, when genetically deleted, had an effect on heart looping formation, with the strongest effect for Metrnla and Metrn.
source: All three paralogs analyzed, when genetically deleted, had an effect on heart looping formation, with the strongest effect for Metrnla and Metrn, while Metrnlb had a smaller but still significant effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of heart looping phenotypes in single mutants showing varying degrees of penetrance.

claim: Metrns play a crucial role in the genetic interaction with integrins ItgαV1 and Itgβ1b for proper clustering and migration of DFCs.
source: We show that Metrns play a crucial role in ensuring this function, the genetic interaction with the integrins ItgαV1 and Itgβ1b, known to facilitate the proper clustering and migration of DFCs based on the sufficient accumulation of ZO-1 and apical constriction, essential to form the KV (Oteíza et al., 2008; Ablooglu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction experiments showing enhanced DFC defects when combining metrn mutations with integrin knockdown.

claim: Metrns are essential for several aspects of KV formation and function, including cilia length, cilia number, KV size, and lumen formation.
source: Furthermore, our results reveal that Metrns are essential for several aspects of the KV formation and function, including the cilia length, cilia number, KV size, and lumen formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of KV parameters showing significant reductions in all measured aspects in triplMut embryos.

claim: Metrns are important for the regulation of proper expression of Nodal flow genes.
source: Consequently, Metrns are important for the regulation of the proper expression of Nodal flow genes, and this regulation is critical for the proper asymmetric positioning and morphology of vital organs like the heart (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR and in situ hybridization data showing altered expression of Nodal pathway genes in metrn mutants.

claim: Zebrafish midline mutants display altered lft1 and lft2 expression patterns as well as discordance among heart, gut, and brain gene expression patterns.
source: Previous work has shown that zebrafish midline mutants display altered lft1 and lft2 expression patterns as well as discordance among heart, gut, and brain gene expression patterns (Bisgrove et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bisgrove et al., 2000, describing phenotypes of midline mutants.

claim: The body asymmetry defects in triplMut embryos do not originate from impaired midline structures but rather from impaired DFC clustering and migration.
source: Despite the expression of both paralogs close to or at the midline, we hypothesize that the described body asymmetry defects in triplMut embryos do not originate from impaired midline structures but rather impaired DFC clustering and migration. Indeed, triplMut-/- embryos display intact tbxta-positive notochords (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), as well as randomized visceral organs positioning (Figure 1D–E), phenotypes that are not characteristic for defects of the anterior midline (Bisgrove et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that triplMut embryos have intact notochords and randomized organ positioning, which differs from typical midline mutant phenotypes.

claim: DFCs are precursors of the zebrafish KV, essential for left-right axis establishment.
source: DFCs are precursors of the zebrafish KV, organ of laterality, essential for the L-R axis establishment.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the developmental origin and function of the Kupffer's vesicle.

claim: DFCs develop at the beginning of gastrulation and form the KV by the end of gastrulation.
source: DFCs develop at the beginning of gastrulation and form the KV by the end of gastrulation (Essner et al., 2005; Cooper and D'Amico, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Essner et al., 2005 and Cooper and D'Amico, 1996, describing the timeline of DFC development and KV formation.

claim: Metrn-/-, metrnla-/-, and triplMut zebrafish embryos displayed DFC assembly defects and delayed migration during gastrulation.
source: Metrn-/-, metrnla-/-, and triplMut zebrafish embryos displayed DFC assembly defects and delayed migration of these cells during gastrulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization and live imaging data showing DFC clustering and migration defects in metrn mutants.

claim: DFCs in triplMut still express DFC-specific markers (sox17, sox32, tbxta).
source: Since DFCs in triplMut still express DFC-specific markers (sox17, sox32, tbxta), we concluded that Metrns are not required for the specification of DFCs per se, but rather that Metrns are important for their proper clustering and migration.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing continued expression of DFC markers in triplMut embryos.

claim: Metrns are not required for the specification of DFCs per se, but are important for their proper clustering and migration.
source: Since DFCs in triplMut still express DFC-specific markers (sox17, sox32, tbxta), we concluded that Metrns are not required for the specification of DFCs per se, but rather that Metrns are important for their proper clustering and migration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that DFC markers are expressed in triplMut embryos despite clustering and migration defects.

claim: The observed DFC clustering and migration abnormalities in Metrn mutants primarily affect the apico-ventral axis rather than the mediolateral axis.
source: It is important to note that the observed DFC clustering and migration abnormalities in Metrn mutants primarily affect the apico-ventral axis rather than the mediolateral axis. This is evident from the disrupted connection between DFCs and the YSL/EVL in these mutants, while the migration directionality remains intact.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that DFCs maintain directional migration but show defects in EVL attachment and apico-ventral positioning.

claim: Metrns are involved in the polarization and establishment of direct apical contacts of DFCs with the EVL.
source: Since a proper connection between DFCs and the EVL facilitates a subset of DFCs to establish apical contacts with the EVL and become pre-polarized, one could speculate that Metrns are involved in the polarization and establishment of direct apical contacts of DFCs with the EVL (Oteíza et al., 2008; Cooper and D'Amico, 1996; Pulgar et al., 2021; Solnica-Krezel et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observed loss of DFC-EVL connections in metrn mutants and the known role of these connections in DFC polarization.

claim: The loss of apical attachments in metrn mutant embryos causes all DFCs to converge less and migrate more slowly than in wild-type controls.
source: Therefore, the loss of apical attachments in the mutant embryos causes all DFCs to converge less and migrate more slowly than in wild-type controls, as shown by our in vivo imaging analysis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations of reduced DFC-EVL attachment, decreased convergence, and slower migration in triplMut embryos.

claim: A number of DFCs in metrn mutants were too slow to reach the vegetal pole in time to form a fully functional KV.
source: This would imply that a number of DFCs was simply too slow to reach the vegetal pole in time to form a fully functional KV.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observed migration delays and reduced KV cell numbers in triplMut embryos.

claim: KV cilia are monocilia.
source: Given that KV cilia are monocilia, this subsequently results in a diminished count of KV cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), along with the observed structural abnormalities in the KV lumen and impairments in its overall functionality.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the ciliary structure of KV cells.

claim: The formation of the developing KV lumen is directly connected to ciliogenesis as polarized DFCs initiate developing cilia at their membrane domain facing the forming lumen.
source: Additionally, it was shown that the formation of the developing KV lumen was directly connected to ciliogenesis as polarized DFCs initiate developing cilia at their membrane domain facing the forming lumen (Oteíza et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Oteíza et al., 2008, describing the relationship between DFC polarization and ciliogenesis.

claim: Proper DFC polarization is essential for KV formation and for ciliogenesis.
source: This indicates that proper DFC polarization is essential for KV formation and for ciliogenesis.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the requirements for KV formation and ciliogenesis.

claim: The reduced cilia length and lack of PKCζ staining in the developing KV of metrns mutants highlight an impairment of DFC polarization.
source: In metrns mutants, the reduced cilia length and the lack of PKCζ staining in the developing KV further highlight an impairment of DFC polarization in the absence of Metrns, consequently leading to KV formation and function defects.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed defects in cilia length and aPKC-ζ staining in triplMut embryos, which are indicators of polarization defects.

claim: Appropriate asymmetrical Nodal flow plays a crucial role in the asymmetrical expression of Nodal genes such as dand5, spaw, lefty1 (lft1), and lefty2 (lft2).
source: It has been demonstrated that appropriate asymmetrical Nodal flow plays a crucial role in the asymmetrical expression of Nodal genes such as dand5, spaw, lefty1 (lft1), and lefty2 (lft2) (Hirokawa et al., 2006; Harvey, 1998; Hashimoto et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hirokawa et al., 2006, Harvey, 1998, and Hashimoto et al., 2004, describing the relationship between Nodal flow and gene expression.

claim: The disrupted formation and function of the KV in metrns mutants contributes to the perturbation in Nodal factor expression.
source: As such, the disrupted formation and function of the KV in metrns mutants might contribute to the evident perturbation in Nodal factor expression and may also induce randomization of Nodal factor expression in L-R asymmetry (Essner et al., 2005; Nonaka et al., 1998; Gokey et al., 2016; Ablooglu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed KV defects and altered Nodal gene expression in metrn mutants, supported by citations describing the relationship between KV function and Nodal signaling.

claim: Metrns may directly impact the expression of spaw, leftys, and dand5 in addition to their role in DFC cell behaviors and KV formation.
source: We do not exclude, however, that Metrns directly impact the expression of spaw, leftys, and dand5 in addition to their role in DFC cell behaviors and KV formation.
evidence: The claim is speculative, acknowledging the possibility of direct transcriptional regulation by Metrns in addition to their effects on KV formation.

claim: Meteorin was reported as a regulator of mesendoderm development through the enhancement of nodal expression.
source: One of the earliest functions attributed to Meteorin was as a regulator of mesendoderm development through the enhancement of nodal expression (Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2014, describing Meteorin's role in nodal expression regulation.

claim: Nodal signaling regulates DFC specification.
source: In this context, several studies have reported that Nodal signaling was shown to regulate DFC specification (Oteiza et al., 2010; Choi et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Oteiza et al., 2010 and Choi et al., 2007, describing the role of Nodal signaling in DFC specification.

claim: Knockdown of Integrin αV and Integrin β1b in zebrafish results in left-right asymmetry defects.
source: In line with the impaired KV formation and function that we observed in metrns mutants, it was shown that knockdown of Integrin αV as well as Integrin β1b in zebrafish results in L-R asymmetry defects (Ablooglu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ablooglu et al., 2010, describing left-right asymmetry defects in integrin morphants.

claim: Knockdown of Integrin αV and Integrin β1b results in DFC organization and migration defects and disturbed KV formation.
source: This was explained by DFC organization and migration defects and disturbed KV formation.
evidence: The claim is based on the explanation provided in Ablooglu et al., 2010 for the left-right asymmetry defects observed in integrin morphants.

claim: IntegrinαVβ1 specific functions have not yet been completely resolved in mammals due to their broad expression and redundant function with other integrins.
source: IntegrinαVβ1 specific functions have not yet been completely resolved in mammals, mostly due to their broad expression and redundant function with other integrins, as well as the lack of antibodies and inhibitors specific for αVβ1.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the challenges in studying integrin αVβ1 function in mammals.

claim: αVβ1 was shown to be implicated in embryonic astrocytes and oligodendrocyte precursors migration in rodents.
source: For instance, αVβ1 was shown to be implicated in embryonic astrocytes and oligodendrocyte precursors migration in rodents (Milner et al., 1996) and neural cell adhesion molecule L1 cell binding (Felding-Habermann et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Milner et al., 1996, describing the role of αVβ1 in neural cell migration.

claim: αVβ1 is implicated in neural cell adhesion molecule L1 cell binding.
source: For instance, αVβ1 was shown to be implicated in embryonic astrocytes and oligodendrocyte precursors migration in rodents (Milner et al., 1996) and neural cell adhesion molecule L1 cell binding (Felding-Habermann et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Felding-Habermann et al., 1997, describing the role of αVβ1 in L1 binding.

claim: Mechanisms underlying left-right patterning are highly conserved within vertebrates.
